Blending tech finesse  
with market relevance
Our advanced engineering capabilities span a 
comprehensive portfolio of air-cooled and liquid-
cooled engines ranging from 3 kVA to 12,000 kVA, 
enabling us to serve applications of every scale and 
complexity. From industrial operations and critical 
infrastructure specialised power needs, we deliver 
customised solutions designed for performance, 
durability and efficiency.
Driven by dedicated Corporate Research & 
Engineering (CRE) and Application Engineering (AE) 
divisions, our innovation ecosystem is focused on 
anticipating the future. We engineer application-
specific solutions, blending technical precision with 
market relevance for specific requirements. This 
helps us stay agile in a world of spiralling demand  
for performance.
Sustainability is integral to our vision. Our portfolio 
includes emission-compliant and environmentally 
responsible technologies, while our leadership in 
alternative fuels such as biodiesel, natural gas, 
HFEC* and biogas-based engines, underscores our 
commitment to cleaner energy pathways. We are 
also advancing fuel-agnostic and hybrid genset 
technologies that offer greater flexibility, resilience 
and lower environmental impact.
Digital intelligence is redefining performance, and 
Kirloskar is at the forefront of this transformation. 
Through IoT-enabled gensets, predictive remote 
monitoring systems, microgrid solutions and 
intelligent controllers such as Optiprime, we are 
helping customers optimise uptime, efficiency and 
control.
Our engineering ambit has a robust after-sales 
system supported by an extensive service and 
distribution network. Whether enabling high-
horsepower industrial applications or empowering 
farmers with accessible mechanisation solutions, 
we remain committed to engineering outcomes that 
create lasting value.
As we move forward, Kirloskar Oil Engines Limited 
continues to engineer the future of performance, 
with innovation in our thinking, sustainability in our 
approach, and trust in everything proudly Made in 
Kirloskar.

About the report
We are pleased to present our Annual Report which 
includes voluntary information to the extent available 
to us, in accordance with the reporting framework 
developed and designed by International Integrated 
Reporting Council (IIRC). 
This report is primarily intended to address the 
information requirements of investors (our equity and 
prospective investors). Our endeavour is to present 
this information in a manner that is also relevant to all 
the key stakeholders. This report also aligns with the 
Companies Act, 2013, Indian Accounting Standards 
and SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015.
Scope and boundary
This report provides comprehensive information about the business 
activities of Kirloskar Oil Engines Limited (KOEL), suitably communicated 
through the six strategic goals  as per the guidelines defined by the 
International Integrated Reporting Council (IIRC). 
The document encapsulates our business model, overarching performance 
and corresponding results. It is important to note that the financial capital 
parameters discussed in this report pertain exclusively to ‘Kirloskar Oil 
Engines Limited’ on a standalone operation.
Reporting period
The major reporting period for the Annual Report is April 1st, 2025 to 
March 31st, 2026. However, certain portions of the report provide facts and 
numbers from prior years in order to give readers a complete picture.
Assurance for financial statements
To ensure the integrity of facts and information, the financial statements 
are audited by M/s. G. D. Apte & Co., Chartered Accountants. In addition, 
the ‘Independent Auditor’s Report’ has been duly incorporated as part of 
this report.
Stakeholder engagement and materiality 
Stakeholder consultation is central to KOEL's approach to identifying and 
managing material topics, risks and opportunities. Following a materiality 
reassessment in CY 25, stakeholder engagement was carried out primarily 
through structured surveys, designed to capture perceptions on the 
importance of identified environmental, social and governance topics. Inputs 
received through the stakeholder engagement process were analysed using 
a defined scoring to develop a materiality matrix that continues to guide 
KOEL's evolving Sustainability Strategy 2030.

Years of 
excellence
For over 137 years, the Kirloskar Group has served as a keystone of India’s industrial 
evolution. Its journey began in 1888 by a forward-thinking founder who transitioned 
from running a modest bicycle repair shop into creating the nation’s first iron plough, 
an act that laid the foundation for India’s industrial revolution. This pioneering spirit 
catalysed a legacy of progress that continues today. Today, the Group is a distinguished 
leader across multiple sectors—including internal combustion engines, power backup, 
castings, and pneumatic and cooling systems providing critical engineering solutions to 
a diverse global market.
Engineering solutions for 
future generations
The Group provides the backbone of infrastructure across 
a wide variety of sectors, including hospitality, IT/ITES, 
agriculture, manufacturing, food and beverage, oil and gas, 
infrastructure, and real estate. Kirloskar’s remarkable growth 
and resilience are rooted in strong values that serve as the 
establishment for every one of its enterprises.
The Group’s journey began when the founder, Shri Laxmanrao 
Kirloskar, established an ordinary bicycle repair shop in 
Belgaum, Karnataka. This humble start soon transitioned 
into a machine tool workshop, where he created iron 
ploughs and chaff cutters, revolutionary examples of 
engineering advancements that would eventually define the 
Group’s trajectory.
KIRLOSKAR GROUP'S PHILOSOPHY
His son, Shri Shantanurao Laxmanrao Kirloskar, carried this 
legacy forward with visionary leadership, transforming the 
Kirloskar Group into one of India’s most respected industrial 
powerhouses. Under his expert guidance, the Group expanded 
into new sectors and international markets, solidifying the 
Company's reputation on the global stage. 
Today, Shri Laxmanrao Kirloskar is remembered as both 
a pioneer of Indian industry and a reformer dedicated to 
improving lives. His entrepreneurial spirit continues to provide 
opportunities for thousands across India and benefits millions 
more through the Group’s extensive global operations.

Structural actions: Sharpening focus 
for the next phase 
Two important corporate actions were completed in 
FY 25-26:
First, the transfer of our B2C business to our wholly 
owned subsidiary LGM via slump sale was effected 
from Q3 (now branded Kirloskar Fluid Dynamics). 
This sharpens KOEL’s standalone focus on its B2B 
engineering and power generation core, while giving 
Kirloskar Fluid Dynamics — which delivered 10% 
domestic and 13% international growth in  
Q4 FY 25-26 and 36% international revenue growth 
for the full year — the dedicated management 
attention and operational structure suited to its 
distinct market dynamics.
Second, we incorporated Kirloskar Advanced 
Systems Pvt. Ltd. as a new subsidiary, focused on 
systems integration and advanced technology for 
defence and other strategic sectors. Carving this 
into a dedicated entity — with its own governance, 
culture, and accountability — allows us to attract 
specialised talent, and build intellectual property that 
is held separately. We will provide further updates on 
this entity as our programmes mature.
Capacity investment: Building for 
demand already at hand 
The Board has approved two sequential capacity 
investments at our Kagal manufacturing site 
investments driven by demand we are already 
experiencing, not by speculation:
Phase 1: ₹ 700 crores to add engine capacity across 
enhanced and new lines on the existing campus, 
coming online by April 2027. Phase 2: ₹ 1,400 crores 
over two years for an additional high-horsepower and 
specialised engines in a new building at the same site.
Together, these investments ensure KOEL has the 
manufacturing depth to service the opportunities it 
has earned in the High Horsepower, Optiprime,  
and other segments.

deliberate channel building, product certification, and

People, culture
None of what we have achieved is possible 
without our people. This year we made significant 
investments in engineering and product development 
headcount, and our leadership talent processes 
have been strengthened to ensure organisational 
capability scales with our ambitions. Our strategy 
rests on three pillars: attracting the right engineering 
talent by building KOEL’s reputation as a world-class 
environment for solving hard problems; developing 
in-house capability through structured programmes 
that build institutional knowledge; and fostering a 
culture of accountability and innovation.
Technology
On technology, our focus on non-ICE platforms is 
deliberate and measured; we are building capability 
that gives us optionality as the energy landscape 
evolves, not rushing to pivot. 
We are closely monitoring our progress on the four 
technology tracks defined in our growth plan: the ICE 
track, where we continue advancing fuel flexibility 
from natural gas and hydrogen blends towards 
hydrogen; Energy Storage Solutions, where we are 
tracking the evolution across battery chemistries 
to identify integration opportunities; Electrification, 
spanning electric motors and power electronic 
controllers in readiness for hybrid and traction 
applications; and Fuel Cells and Electrolysers, 
where we are building foundational capability in the 
hydrogen economy.
Across all four tracks, our 
approach is consistent: invest in 
understanding, build selective 
capability, and scale when market 
and technology conditions align 
with our core strengths.
Sustainability
KOEL’s approach to sustainability is rooted in the 
belief that what is good for the community and the 
planet is also good for the business over the long run. 
In FY 25-26, we expanded our BRSR disclosures to 
provide stakeholders with deeper visibility into our 
environmental, social and governance performance. 
Energy efficiency improvements across our plants, 
water conservation, waste management, and 
responsible sourcing remained active priorities.
Dividend
Reflecting our confidence in the sustained earnings 
power of the business, the Board of Directors 
proposed a total dividend of 350% for the fiscal year. 
This includes a final dividend of 225% which is ₹ 4.50 
per share subject to shareholders’ approval,  
in addition to the interim dividend of 125%, i.e  
₹ 2.50 per share.
India’s macro tailwinds and our path  
to $2 billion 
India is at an inflection point. Infrastructure 
spending is at a multi-decade high. Data centers, 
semiconductor fabs, defence manufacturing, smart 
cities, tier-2 and tier-3 real estate development, and 
the energy transition are creating sustained, multi-
year demand for reliable power. The Make in India 
and Atmanirbhar Bharat agenda is simultaneously 
creating structural opportunities in Defence, Railways 
and Nuclear — sectors where KOEL has established 
genuine product and relationship credentials.
We have an aspiration to reach $2 billion in revenue 
by FY 29-30. Our performance over the last four 
years demonstrates that this is possible. The journey 
will require continued product innovation, deeper 
market penetration domestically and internationally, 
disciplined execution on our large order backlog in 
Nuclear and Defence, and the successful ramp-
up of our Kagal expansion. It will also require us to 
build the organisation — the people, the systems, 
and the culture that a $2 billion global engineering 
company needs.
We are building KOEL to last — not to perform for 
one cycle, but to be a company that is relevant, 
competitive, and trusted across generations. That 
is the standard we hold ourselves to, and that is the 
standard we invite you to hold us to.
On behalf of the Board of Directors and the leadership

suppliers, customers, and shareholders for the trust 
you have placed in us. We will honour that trust by 
continuing to build KOEL into the global engineering 
institution it is destined to become.

The space and variable load dilemma
Modern industrial facilities, commercial complexes and critical 
infrastructure increasingly face the challenge of meeting 
growing power requirements while operating within a limited 
space. Conventional standby power systems often require 
multiple large gensets and extensive installation spaces, making 
it difficult to deploy them in high-density urban developments, 
data centers and industrial facilities. 
Engineered to minimise space, 
maximise power
KOEL engineered the Optiprime series as an ultra-compact, 
export-grade power solution that delivers high output from a 
significantly reduced space, enabling customers to optimise 
valuable space without compromising reliability or performance.
At the heart of the Optiprime range lies its patented Twin Hybrid 
Power Pack architecture, which integrates two synchronised 
power cores within a single compact system. It maximises 
power density while reducing the space requirements. The 
hybrid architecture continuously monitors load conditions 
and automatically distributes power between the two cores 
to match the demand efficiently. The result is a solution that 
combines space optimisation, operational flexibility and built-
in redundancy. During maintenance or servicing of one power 
core, the other seamlessly supports critical loads, ensuring 
uninterrupted power availability.
Last-mile customisation
To meet diverse global compliance demands, KOEL engineered 
the complete system as a  highly flexible single-package asset. 
By consolidating power cores, internal synchronisation systems, 
and post-treatment exhaust into a single enclosure, the system 
simplifies international transportation and field installation. This 
compact design gives project  architects the freedom to execute 
last-mile site customisation, tailoring acoustic insulation for 
strict urban noise limits or tweaking layouts for irregular physical 
spaces. This modular adaptability makes it equally effective for 
urban commercial high-rises and remote, rural utilities.
Green solutions and positive returns 
In an industrial landscape repurposed for decarbonisation, the 
Optiprime series proves that ecological responsibility can align 
with financial prudence. Fully compliant with advanced CPCB IV+ 
emission standards, the system relies on specialised emission 
control technology to minimise its environmental footprint. 
By keeping the engine within its optimal thermal efficiency 
band, the system delivers superior fuel economy. This massive 
reduction in operating expenditure (opex) directly accelerates 
recovery of capital expenditure (capex), offering global 
organisations a highly sustainable power solution with the 
shortest timeline for a positive ROI.

Every business decision is taken with a thorough understanding of 
associated risks and a conscious acceptance of their implications.
Our risk approach is built to safeguard and strengthen business 
value by proactively addressing uncertainties and minimising 
potential adverse outcomes.
We foster a culture where every employee understands the risks 
relevant to their role and is equipped with the knowledge to address 
and manage them effectively.
The controls and measures we deploy are designed for sustained 
impact, embedded directly into our core business processes rather 
than treated as isolated interventions.
Our risk tolerance thresholds are periodically revisited and 
recalibrated to remain aligned with the evolving direction and 
priorities of the organisation.
All risk events — whether emerging, ongoing, or resolved — are 
reported in a timely manner, with appropriate and decisive action

higher reliability, faster deployment, tighter compliance

platform to participate in India’s defence modernisation 
with project-specific, reliable power solutions.

Data center expansion
Market context  
India makes up about a fifth of global data consumption but 
hosts less than 5% of the world’s data centers. The industry 
is on a swing. India’s digital infrastructure is expanding rapidly 
with enterprises investing heavily in data center capacity. It 
is estimated that India’s data center capacity is expected to 
grow from 1.5 GW in 2025 to 8–10 GW by 2030. Unlike most 
commercial applications, data centers operate under strict 
uptime requirements and cannot tolerate grid instability, 
making high-capacity backup power not a discretionary 
purchase but a core infrastructure requirement. 
Impact  
This non-discretionary nature of demand, combined with 
the scale and speed of data center investment across the 
country, is creating powerful and sustained tailwinds for 
premium, high kVA gensets. 
Push for indigenisation and infrastructure
Market context  
Government policy is playing an increasingly significant role in 
shaping the demand pattern in the industrial sector. Make-in-
India initiatives in defence, railways, and marine are driving a 
strong preference for domestically manufactured equipment. 
The government’s sustained commitment to investing in 
infrastructure across roadways, ports, energy systems, 
and urban development is generating large, long-duration 
project opportunities. 
Impact  
These policy-driven segments share common traits such 
as meaningful entry barriers in the form of technical 
certifications and indigenisation requirements that strictly 
limit the pool of suppliers, ensuring credibility. For companies 
that qualify, this translates into the access to high-value, 
relatively stable demand that is less exposed to the 
competitive intensity of open-market segments.
Our response
We have made targeted investments in the capabilities 
and certifications required to compete credibly in 
defence, railways, and marine applications, developing 
indigenised product variants that meet the specific 
requirements of government procurement frameworks. 
The Company has partnerships with government 
agencies and PSUs to build the reputation and 
track record needed to capture a growing share of 
infrastructure-linked demand — a segment that we 
view as an important source of high-quality, long-
cycle revenue.
Our response
We have made the data center segment a strategic priority, 
treating data center expansion as a large opportunity in  
high-capacity, premium gensets.
External environment
Stricter environmental scrutiny and decarbonisation push
Market context  
Beyond CPCB IV+, the broader trajectory of environmental 
regulation and corporate sustainability commitments 
is placing increasing pressure on diesel-based power 
generation. Consumers across sectors are facing growing 
scrutiny and this is beginning to shift the purchasing 
decisions in favour of lower-emission and hybrid power 
solutions. As a result, gas-based gensets and hybrid, 
solar and DG, configurations are emerging as the most 
immediate alternatives. 
Impact  
For the genset industry, this trend creates both a challenge 
and an opportunity. Manufacturers that remain anchored 
to conventional diesel products face the risk of gradual 
loss of demand as customers pursue greener alternatives. 
Those that invest in alternative technologies can position 
themselves to lead the next generation of the market, 
capturing early-mover advantage in segments that are 
growing rapidly and carry higher margins.
Our response
KOEL has chosen to treat the alternate energy push 
as a strategic opportunity, instead of a threat. We 
have launched hybrid Optiprime series and it is 
gaining commercial traction and are investing in the 
development of hydrogen-ready systems to ensure 
it is positioned for the longer-term evolution of the 
market. We also provide engines designed to run on

environmental responsibility and the increasing influence of 
climate-related regulatory and transition risks to our operations 
and product portfolio. Actual positive impacts include improved

market competitiveness from the development of low-emission 
and fuel-agnostic products, including the installation of

The materiality assessment recognised that as we scale 
our operations across geographies and subsidiaries, robust

opportunity to enhance stakeholder trust and long-term value 
creation. Actual impacts include improved investor confidence

mechanisms, while potential negative impacts include regulatory 
penalties and reputational harm from gaps in governance.

Board roles and responsibilities, independent committees,

enterprise risk management, vigil mechanisms, and continuous 
regulatory monitoring.
Business ethics
The materiality assessment recognised that as we operate 
across domestic and international markets with a wide 
network of business relationships, maintaining ethical 
conduct is fundamental to business continuity, reputation, and 
compliance. Actual impacts include stronger stakeholder trust 
and disciplined decision-making through a stringent ethical 
culture, while potential negative impacts include financial losses, 
penalties, and reputational damage arising from lapses such as 
fraud, conflicts of interest, or non-compliance with the Code 
of Conduct. 
This topic was prioritised based on its broad applicability 
across the organisation and its direct bearing on our licence to 
operate. We manage this through a Code of Conduct applicable 
to Directors, employees, and suppliers, supported by structured 
policies on related party transactions, insider trading, whistle-
blower protection, and mandatory training, ensuring early 
identification and resolution of ethical concerns.
Occupational health and safety
The materiality assessment reflected the significance of 
occupational health and safety across machinery-intensive 
manufacturing facilities and field service operations. 
Stakeholder inputs, including those from employees and senior 
leadership, highlighted the direct link between workplace safety 
and operational resilience. Positive impacts include enhanced 
employee wellbeing, workforce productivity, and our record of 
zero injuries and fatalities across plants in the previous financial 
year. Potential negative impacts could be injuries, operational 
disruptions, regulatory non-compliance, and reputational harm 
from inadequate safety practices. 
This topic was prioritised based on its high relevance to human 
rights and employee welfare, as well as the regulatory and 
financial consequences of safety failures. We manage this 
through environmental, occupational health and safety policies, 
ISO 45001-aligned safety management systems, periodic audits, 
emergency preparedness drills, hands-on training on PPE and 
fire safety, and an embedded safety reporting culture.
Sustainable innovation
The materiality assessment recognised that tightening emission 
norms, technological advancement, and our strategic transition 
from a diesel-centric portfolio to a diversified energy solutions 
model make sustained innovation essential for regulatory 
readiness and competitiveness. Actual positive impacts 
include differentiated product offerings, improved emissions 
compliance, and stronger long-term market positioning, 
while potential negative impacts from delayed or inadequate 
innovation include increased compliance costs, loss of market 
access, and reduced competitiveness. 
This topic was prioritised as an opportunity, given its direct 
connection to our strategic transformation and future revenue 
potential. We manage this through structured in-house R&D 
investments, a technology roadmap focused on alternate fuels, 
emission-compliant platforms, modular designs, and digital 
integration with strong governance oversight ensuring alignment 
between innovation, manufacturing, and market objectives.
Circular economy
Circular economy was identified as a material topic through 
our 2026 materiality assessment, informed by stakeholder 
expectations around responsible resource use, intensifying 
regulatory focus on waste and material efficiency, and the 
environmental footprint of our manufacturing-intensive 
operations. Actual positive impacts include cost savings, 
reduced resource dependency, and lower environmental impact 
through practices such as 100% reuse of treated wastewater 
and plastic-to-fuel conversion. Potential negative impacts from 
inadequate circular practices include higher operating costs, 
regulatory non-compliance, and reputational risk arising from 
inefficient waste management or excess use of virgin materials.

Smart energy monitoring

energy-efficient compressors and SCADA-based solutions to 
enhance our ability to forecast, schedule, and regulate energy

agnostic and alternative-fuel engines and gensets compliant

Due to the strict mandate, lower particulate matter, and NOx 
emissions for diesel gensets up to 800 kW, it has accelerated 
our transition towards advanced technologies like CRDI systems, 
after-treatment solutions, and dual-fuel configurations.
Driving circularity: LCA and waste stewardship
Following our FY 24-25 Life Cycle Assessment on our highest-volume engine platform, KOEL actively drives circularity 
through two key waste initiatives. First, the Kirloskar Nulife programme remanufactures field-returned engines to strict 
quality standards, extending lifespans and supporting customer carbon reduction. Second, the Company relies on recyclable 
packaging and metallic skids, whilst fully complying with Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) targets for plastic packaging 
and battery waste management.
Energy transition market readiness
Showing a strong commitment to responsible energy 
consumption, the Company balances strict regulatory 
compliance with resource optimisation across its product 
portfolio. By developing electronically controlled engines, 
integrating advanced after-treatment systems, and deploying 
emission-compliant technologies, we continuously minimises 
operational fuel consumption and lifecycle costs. We have 
proven our market readiness for the clean energy transition 
by commercialising alternative fuel solutions, including LPG-
powered gensets for retail use and ethanol-based variants for 
the telecom sector, ensuring eco-efficient performance across 
our entire footprint.
Water management
KOEL has implemented a real-time water monitoring system featuring multiple water flow meters and live tank level sensors to 
track consumption across multiple sources. Centralised oversight through Bullfro Water Management Solutions ensures 24X7 
visibility, while in-house weather stations and piezometers enable efficient management of rainwater harvesting and groundwater 
levels. Additional conservation measures include the use of dry cutting machines in machining processes, reuse of air conditioning 
condensate for coolant preparation and installation of smart urinal O-rings to lower freshwater demand.
At KOEL, 100% of the treated wastewater is reused across manufacturing locations for processes such as flushing and irrigation, 
reducing freshwater withdrawal to support circular economy. We have deployed a 100-LPH Electric Evaporator in the Effluent 
Treatment Plant at its Nashik facility, treating 2 kilolitres of wastewater daily. It lowered our water intensity from 865.55 kL/million 
rupees adjusted to PPP to 696.91 kL/million rupees adjusted to PPP. 
We are transitioning from solvent-based to water-based paints to lower VOC emissions and minimise paint waste toxicity, while lean 
manufacturing reduces raw material, water, and energy consumption at source.

Kagal waste management transformation
Context
In 2024, the Kagal Municipal Council faced challenges in 
waste segregation, landfill dependency, and inefficient waste 
processing. Low source segregation rates and inadequate 
waste management infrastructure highlighted the need for 
improved sanitation, sustainable waste practices, and greater 
community awareness.
KOEL's intervention
As part of its CSR commitment, KOEL partnered with the 
Kagal Municipal Council to strengthen waste management 
and sanitation. The Company supported awareness 
campaigns in schools and communities, promoted 
source segregation, encouraged citizen participation, 
and helped improve waste processing infrastructure and 
operational efficiency.
Outcome
Within one year from August 2024, the initiative delivered 
significant results: the city's cleanliness ranking improved 
from 110th to 12th, source segregation increased from 30% 
to 80%, and waste processing facility Overall Equipment 
Effectiveness (OEE) reached 80%. 
Waste sent to landfills was brought down to zero from three 
loads, supporting a zero-landfill approach. The initiative also 
strengthened community awareness on waste management 
and earned KOEL a Gratitude Letter from the Kagal 
Municipal Council.
Strategic impact
The initiative demonstrates the power of industry-
government collaboration in advancing sustainable urban 
development. By improving waste segregation, eliminating 
landfill disposal, enhancing operational efficiency, and 
building community awareness, KOEL created a scalable 
waste management model aligned with circular economy 
principles and strengthened environmental stewardship in 
semi-urban India.

Kagal biodiversity project
At KOEL, we are deeply committed to ensuring environmental 
sustainability and fostering climate resilience through the 
systematic enrichment of natural habitats and the holistic 
rejuvenation of local water bodies. Our initiatives at the Kagal 
Biodiversity Park focus on an intensive native plantation 
strategy, specifically designed to breathe new life into the 
ecosystem by introducing a rich matrix of indigenous flora 
that strengthens local bird and butterfly populations. A major 
cornerstone of this programme is the ecological restoration of 
the park's natural stream (nala) trajectories and water margins, 
where we are planting specialised, deep-rooting native species 
like Jamun, Arjun, and Erythrina to anchor soil banks, naturally 
filter water, and establish vital riparian corridors.
By collaborating with local institutions like the Forest 
Department nursery and the Naoroji Godrej Centre for Plant 
Research (NGCPR) to source climate-habituated, locally 
acclimated saplings, this initiative maximises plant survival rates 
and accelerates the recovery of the natural watershed.

With a customer-centric approach, a seasoned management

significant growth since the inception of operations in fiscal 
year 2020. It operates in 3 main business segments: SME 
Lending, Wholesale Lending and recently launched Secured 
Retail Financing.
	
The launch of our Secured Retail vertical represents a defining 
shift in Arka Fincap’s strategy, prioritising asset granularity 
and long-term balance sheet stability. As a primary growth 
catalyst, this segment leverages Secured Business Loans 
and Pre-Owned Wheels financing to bridge the credit gap for 
the MSME sector, fostering a more diversified and resilient 
portfolio. The speed of execution in Secured Retail has been 
remarkable; within a single year, we established a presence 
across 7 states with a robust network of 100+ Secured Retail 
branches. This rapid scale-up is powered by a dedicated 
team of over 1,000 retail professionals whose local insights 
have driven deep market penetration. Strategically, the retail 
segment now contributes ~9% of Arka’s total AUM. More 
importantly, it is fundamentally shifting our asset composition 
toward greater granularity. By reducing concentration risk 
and increasing the number of touchpoints, we are building a 
scalable foundation that ensures long-term stability.

or complete capital infusion. With a keen focus on catering to 
the requirements of its esteemed clients, the division ensures 
a smooth and seamless process from initiation to completion. 
Syndication business offers comprehensive solutions to 
corporate clients encompassing project finance, capital 
expenditure, general corporate needs, last mile financing, 
and subordinated structured debt. Through advisory, 
syndicating, selldown, and co-lending strategies spanning 
various sectors, it ensures tailored financial assistance for 
every requirement.

achieving a 9.5% y-o-y growth in AUM to reach ₹ 7,947 Crores.

increasing granularity, ensuring a high-quality and resilient

13.	Risk Management, Internal Audit and 
Internal Control Framework
	
The Board recognises the importance of sound internal 
controls and risk management practices to good corporate 
governance. The Board is responsible for the governance of 
risk and ensures that management maintains a sound system 
of risk management and internal controls, to safeguard the 
interests of the Company and its shareholders. All material 
decisions of the Board take into relevant consideration the 
nature and extent of risks which the Company is willing to take 
in achieving its strategic objectives and value creation. The 
Company’s internal control system is commensurate with 
the nature of the business, size and complexity of operations 
covering all businesses and functions of the organisation. In line 
with the commitment of a high standard of compliance with 
accounting, financial reporting, internal controls, corporate 
governance and auditing requirements and any legislation 
relating thereto, the Company has a Code of Business Conduct 
applicable to Company personnel covering a wide range of 
business practices and procedures. This includes, but is 
not limited to, compliance with laws, rules and regulations, 
avoidance of conflicts of interests, practicing ethical behavior, 
ensuring integrity of financial statements, protection of 
information, intellectual property and technology, diversity 
and inclusion and prevention of harassment and violence. 
The Company’s risk management process is designed to 
facilitate identification, evaluation, mitigation and review of 
risks which may affect achievement of objectives. It is aligned 
with the strategy deployment processes of the organisation. 
A risk-based audit plan on a yearly basis is approved by the 
Audit Committee. Significant observations and progress of 
implementation of the action plan are reported to and reviewed 
by the Audit Committee. The enterprise risks and their 
mitigation plans are presented by the risk owners to the Risk 
Management Committee. The Enterprise Risk Management 
(“ERM”) framework is aimed at effectively mitigating the 
business and enterprise risks through strategic actions. The 
mitigation plans for enterprise and business risks are reviewed 
and updated on a periodic basis to the Risk Management, 
Audit Committee and the Board of Directors of the Company. 
The risk management process which has been established 
across the Company, addresses major types of risks which 
are at enterprise and business level. The risks are reviewed 
with respect to the likelihood and impact following a balanced 
bottom-up and top-down approach covering all businesses 
and functions of the Company. The review of the risks is done 
based on changes in the external environment, which have a

A.	 Conservation of Energy
	
The coming year, our commitment to efficiency and 
environmental responsibility takes on a new urgency. The 
recent, stricter government pollution norms, such as the CPCB 
IV+, Bharat Stage VI emission norms and Corporate Average 
Fuel Efficiency (“CAFE”) standards, are not just regulatory 
requirements; they are a clear call to action for our industry 
and a vital step towards ensuring cleaner air and a healthier 
planet for future generations.
	
As a leader in engine manufacturing, we recognise our 
significant role in this transition. The industrial sector accounts 
for a substantial portion of national energy consumption, 
and our products have a direct impact on environmental 
quality. Therefore, our response to these challenges must be 
proactive and innovative. We can also focus on how our internal 
manufacturing processes can become more energy-efficient 
and compliant with environmental regulations.
	
We at Kirloskar Oil Engines Limited, leverages Environmental, 
Social and Governance (“ESG”) principles to create both 
financial and non-financial value. By prioritising sustainable 
practices like local procurement, recycling and reusing of waste 
etc. KOEL reduces operational costs and enhances efficiency, 
leading to improved financial performance. ESG initiatives 
also strengthen brand reputation, attract socially conscious 
investors, and foster customer loyalty. KOEL's commitment to 
ESG not only drives profitability but also ensures sustainable 
growth, aligning the company with global best practices and 
stakeholder expectations.
	
Identifying and continuing the journey on sustainability, KOEL 
is recognised at State and National level for continuous efforts 
and fantastic results in Energy Conservation drive. KOEL 
once again, emerged as strong leader in Energy and Water 
conservation initiatives and bagged “Excellent Energy efficient 
unit award and National Energy Leader award” organised by CII 
and awarded with “Gold rating in India Green Manufacturing 
Challenge, Diamond trophy for consecutive performance and 
Runner up in APEX and Water awards by CII”.

alternate sources of energy
	
During the Financial Year under review, 49% (10124140 kWh) 
of total electricity energy consumption at Kagal plant, with 
an approximate savings of ₹ 5.59 Crores was through units 
generated from Solar Captive Power Plant and third party 
renewable energy purchase. This includes 1854022 kWh 
electrical units which were purchased through third party open 
access renewable energy purchase mechanism.
	
At Khadki plant, 27% (2080599 kWh) of total electricity energy 
consumption was through Energy purchased from third party.
	
At Nashik plant, 26% (265165 kWh) of total electricity energy 
consumption was through Captive solar power plant with the 
savings of ₹ 30.20 Lakhs.

Management Discussion 
and Analysis
Kirloskar Oil Engines Limited (KOEL) operates in a dynamic environment shaped 
by evolving energy needs, infrastructure growth, and rising focus on efficiency 
and sustainability.
Guided by its ‘Made in Kirloskar’ philosophy, the Company continues 
to advance indigenous engineering, technology-led manufacturing, 
and in-house innovation to deliver reliable, high-performance 
solutions like internal combustion engines and generator sets. 
Its 2B2B vision further strengthens engagement across the value 
chain through closer partnerships with OEMs, EPC players, and 
institutional customers.
During the year, the Company restructured its business by 
transferring its B2C business to KOEL Fluid Dynamics Limited, 
sharpening focus on core B2B (Power & Energy) segments while 
enabling independent growth for the consumer business. It also 
incorporated a wholly owned subsidiary, Kirloskar Advanced 
Systems Pvt. Ltd., marking its strategic entry into high‑growth 
sectors such as defence and railways.
These initiatives reflect a calibrated shift from a product-centric 
model to a focused, solutions-led structure, positioning KOEL on 
track to create sustainable value and secure long-term growth. This 
section outlines the key industry trends, business performance, 
strategic priorities, and risks and opportunities shaping the 
Company’s outlook.
To strengthen its presence in Africa region, on 11th February, 2026, 
the Company announced that its wholly owned subsidiary Kirloskar 
International ME FZE, UAE ("KIME") will acquire 100% stake in 
Kirloskar Trading SA (PTY) Limited ("KTSPL"). Thus connecting with 
customers more closely and to enable market growth in Powergen 
segment through focus on data center and engineered products 
while enhancing its distribution network in the region.
Economic review
An overview of global economy
The world economy stayed resilient in CY 25, growing  3.4% even 
amid unabated geopolitical crises, scattered trade fragmentations, 
and challenging fiscal conditions. 
3.4%
Global GDP growth rate 
Growth trends remained uneven across regions. While advanced 
economies suffered a steeper slowdown because of policy 
tightening and structural headwinds, emerging markets and 
developing economies managed to pull off relatively stronger 
growth, fuelled by domestic demand and investment activity. 
The US economy was rather resilient on the back of a robust 
consumption and a strong labour market, accelerating 2.2% in 
CY 26. The Eurozone, on its part, made a gradual recovery amid 
continued weakness in manufacturing activities.
Downside risks dominate the global economic outlook. A protracted 
conflict between Ukraine and Russia and extended US-Iran 
war, leading to greater trade fragmentation, a reassessment 
of expectations surrounding AI-driven productivity, or brewing 
trade disputes among major economies may significantly weaken 
the global growth and destabilise the financial market. Elevated 
public debt and eroded institutional credibility made the economy 
more vulnerable1.
With the economic growth likely to average below the pre‑pandemic 
level, the world may skid into a prolonged lower‑growth trajectory 
if policy coordination remains limited. On the other hand, emerging 
economies, particularly those in Asia, are expected to remain the 
key contributors to global growth, with India continuing to stand out 
as one of the fastest‑growing major economies.

Management Discussion and Analysis
Industry overview
Powergen business
Global powergen scenario1
In CY 25, the global power generation landscape was shaped 
by a surge in electricity demand, driven by the rapid growth of 
hyperscale data centers and AI workloads.
The global power generation industry scaled approximately 
$2,072.06 billion in the preceding year.  Expansion of AI-driven 
computing is increasing the demand for high-density, uninterrupted 
power, while continued worldwide adoption of Electric Vehicles 
(EVs) is reshaping distribution requirements.
Even as the transition to renewable energy accelerates, conventional 
generation remains critical for ensuring energy security and 
providing baseline stability for intermittent sources. This ‘dual-
track’ energy mix underscores increasing reliance on fuel-agnostic 
and hybrid systems to balance sustainability with reliability.
Accordingly, the global power generation market is expected to grow 
at 5.2% in CY 26, as countries address the need to upgrade ageing 
energy  infrastructure to support a digital-first, electrified economy.
An evolving regulatory landscape
A stricter regulatory regime of CPCB IV+ was made mandatory in 
July 2024 as part of India’s pledge to go Net Zero on emissions by 
2070. The full implementation of CPCB IV+ guidelines for gensets 
up to 800 kW mandates significant reduction in particulate matter 
and NOx emissions, accelerating the shift towards advanced 
technologies such as CRDI systems, after‑treatment solutions, and 
dual-fuel configurations. 
The CEV Stage V guidelines for construction equipment laid out 
stricter emission standards and advanced filtration technologies, 
while deferring compliance timelines for TREM Stage V tractors 
to balance industry transition. Region-specific mandates, such as 
the 70% gas-based dual-fuel requirement in the NCR, eased the 
transition to cleaner fuels, according to the Commission for Air 
Quality Management (CAQM).
Government policy support in the infrastructure, energy, 
and industrial sectors firmed up long-term demand visibility. 
Investments in railways, defence, and large-scale infrastructure 
projects, along with initiatives such as the National Infrastructure 
Pipeline and manufacturing incentive schemes, supported demand 
for engines and power solutions. Clean energy initiatives, including 
allocations towards nuclear energy, the National Green Hydrogen 
Mission, and PM Surya Ghar Yojana, and Battery Energy Storage 
Systems (BESS), accelerated the shift towards hybrid and low-
carbon energy ecosystems.
Rural and MSME-focused initiatives such as Jal Jeevan Mission, 
PM-KUSUM, and targeted credit programmes supported 
decentralised power demand while gradually reshaping the market 
towards cleaner alternatives.
On the global front, the strained trade ties between the US and 
China over tariff barriers created room for India to emerge as a 
manufacturing and export hub as part of the China+1 strategy of the 
West. Engineering exports, particularly IC engines and components, 
reaped the benefits with a 13% y-o-y growth4.  
At the same time, geopolitical uncertainties and energy transition 
imperatives accelerated investments in alternative fuels and hybrid 
technologies, reaffirming the strategic importance of compliant, 
efficient, and future-ready power solutions. 
A perspective on the Indian economy
India kept up a strong economic momentum since last fiscal, 
expanding  7.7% in FY 25-26, maintaining its position as the fastest-
growing major economy1. The growth was supported by rising 
private consumption, steady agricultural output, improving urban 
and rural demand, and sustained public capital expenditure. 
India’s macroeconomic fundamentals remained stable, with 
investment activities supported by infrastructure spending and 
policy initiatives such as the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) 
scheme and Make-in-India mission. In sync with a robust domestic 
consumption, the country’s industrial activity stayed strong, with 
the Index of Industrial Production (IIP) rising 7.8% in December 
2025 and infrastructure/construction goods growing 12.1%. 
Capital expenditure increased by 10.1% to ₹11.11 lakhs crores in the 
Union Budget 25–26, aiding construction and equipment demand.
Power and infrastructure trends significantly shaped the demand

Industrial business
Global industrial scenario
The global industrial B2B market is projected to reach $11.53 trillion 
by 2030 for physical distribution2. Industrial machinery alone 
is expected to exceed $847 billion by 2030, with the $206 billion 
industrial construction business growing in sync. 
Specialised logistics and safety segments are also expanding 
strongly, averaging 7–10% growth rates with Industry 4.0 
implementation. The sector is undergoing a major transformation 
driven by automation, artificial intelligence (AI), and decarbonisation 
initiatives in North America and Europe. Asia-Pacific and ASEAN 
benefit from supply chain diversification and rising manufacturing, 
infrastructure and investment, while the Middle East gains from 
diversification and giga projects. South America and Africa are led 
by mining demand and agricultural modernisation. 
Asia-Pacific remains the largest market, while North America leads 
in technology integration and advanced industrial adoption.
Indian industrial scenario
The Indian industrial sector is being propelled by significant 
government-led capital expenditure and policy support 
across infrastructure, defence, manufacturing, energy, and 
agriculture. For FY 25-26, the infrastructure outlay was a record 
₹11.21 lakhs crores, equivalent to around 3.1% of the GDP. 
Railways remain a key driver of India's infrastructure development, 
with a capital outlay of ₹2.93 lakhs crores in the Union Budget. 
Together with PM Gati Shakti initiative, this is expected to create 
significant opportunities for the industrial, manufacturing, and 
engineering sectors. 
Defence allocation for FY 26-27 stands at ₹7.85 lakhs crores, 
including a capex of ₹2.19 lakhs crores. Around 75% of the 
modernisation budget is earmarked for domestic procurement. 
Industrial development is further supported by ₹8,658 crores 
already invested in Defence Industrial Corridors, alongside a 
₹53,439 crores potential pipeline. 
The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme, with a total outlay 
of ₹1.91 lakhs crores across 14 sectors, as proposed in the Union 
Budget for FY 26-27, remains a key catalyst for private investment 
into manufacturing. Additional momentum comes from ₹20,000 
crores earmarked for the Nuclear Energy Mission, ₹19,327 crores 
for petroleum and natural gas, ₹3.86 lakhs crores for the National 
Monetisation Pipeline, and ₹1.40 lakhs crores allocated to farm 
sector modernisation in FY 26-27.
The Indian market unleashed strong opportunities across core 
industrial segments in 2026. At $790 billion, construction was 
the primary growth engine, while major ports handled a record 
915 million tonnes of cargo in FY 25-26, and defence exports 
reached a record ₹38,424 crores. 
India also remains the world’s third-largest oil consumer, with the 
sector looking at an investment of $25 billion in exploration and 
production. The country’s nuclear capacity of 8.8 GW stays the 
course to reach 100 GW by 2047, when the government hopes to 
transform India into a developed economy.
Fluid Dynamics (FD)
Fluid management is critical to sustainable growth. The statement 
is validated by a 5% y-o-y growth in the international pump market 
to $64.3 billion. On the home front, the market surged over 6% to $2 
billion, driven by advanced technology, use of AI-powered systems, 
industrial expansion, and subsidies in agriculture, urbanisation, and 
infrastructure development. While the Indian market remains 70% 
agricultural and residential, there is a significant shift towards high-
margin industrial segments, solar adoption, and IoT integration.

KOEL continues to follow a bifurcated market strategy, with both its 
segments facing unique headwinds ranging from regulatory shifts 
to climate-induced volatility.
Engineering and industrial excellence
The business remains KOEL’s primary revenue driver, encompassing 
powergen, industrial engines, and international business. It is 
defined by three critical pressure points:
 
y
Regulatory & emission compliance: The transition to stricter 
emission norms is a non-negotiable hurdle. Failure to align 
product portfolios with these evolving standards poses the 
triple threats of statutory penalties, direct revenue losses 
from barred sales, and a long-term erosion of KOEL's premium 
brand equity.
 
y
Supply chain resilience: Supporting high-precision engineering 
requires a robust, stable supply chain. Any disruption in 
the procurement of critical raw materials or specialised 
components immediately jeopardises production timelines 
and operational efficiency.
 
y
Innovation & competitive differentiation: Operating in a 
high-stakes environment, KOEL faces intense pressure to 
innovate. With global and local players rapidly adopting hybrid 
and alternative fuel technologies, KOEL must sustain its 
‘differentiation edge’ to prevent market share dilution.
Fluid Dynamics (FD)

solutions, and operates under a different set of market stressors:

high density of unorganised players. This leads to aggressive 
price wars, putting constant pressure on KOEL’s margins 
despite its superior distribution network and brand heritage.
 
y

linked to rainfall patterns. An inconsistent monsoon leads to 
significant volatility in demand for pump sets and agricultural 
equipment, making y-o-y revenue forecasting a challenge.

recently integrated its standalone FD business into its 
subsidiary, Pvt. Ltd. (formerly known as La-Gajjar Machineries

synergies and provide the dedicated focus needed to compete 
in the retail landscape.

the way your Company conducts its business. The actions are 
governed by the values and principles of the Company, which 
are reinforced at all levels within the Company.
	
The Company’s Code of Business Conduct, its Risk 
Management Framework together with its well-structured 
internal control systems which are subjected to regular 
assessment for its effectiveness, reinforces integrity of 
Management and fairness in dealing with the Company’s 
stakeholders. This, together with meaningful Corporate Social 
Responsibility activities and sustainable development policies 
followed by the Company has enabled your Company to earn 
the trust and goodwill of its investors, business partners, 
employees and the communities in which it operates.
	
The Company's philosophy of good Corporate Governance 
aims at establishing a system which will assist the 
management to fulfill its corporate objectives as well as 
to serve the best interest of the stakeholders at large viz., 
Shareholders, Customers, Employees, Environment, Society, 
Suppliers, Lenders etc. This philosophy has been strengthened 
by adoption of a Code of Conduct for Board of Directors and 
Senior Management, adoption of CII’s Business Excellence 
framework, Code for prevention of Insider Trading and also re-
enforcing our commitment towards Corporate Sustainability 
and adoption of the Global Reporting Initiative (“GRI”) guidelines 
on Triple Bottom Line reporting.
2.	 Code of Conduct
	
The Company has adopted the Code of Conduct for the Board 
of Directors and Senior Management of the Company in 
accordance with provisions of the SEBI Listing Regulations and 
the Companies Act, 2013, including Rules made thereunder. 
The same is available on the Company’s website (weblink: 
https://www.kirloskaroilengines.com/documents/6887317/
bb0a1acf-7b75-593c-9884-6983b438a34c). It serves 
following objectives:
	
a.	
To enhance the standards of ethical conduct, which are 
based on Kirloskar Group core values.
	
b.	
To evolve as good corporate citizens by implementing 
highest degree of transparency, integrity, accountability 
and corporate social responsibility.
	
c.	
To further achieve good corporate governance 
by complying with all laws, rules, and regulations 
applicable to the company and fulfilling responsibilities 
towards stakeholders.
	
d.	
To set standards of professional conduct for Independent 
Directors on the Board of the Company, with the aim of 
promoting confidence of the investment community, 
minority shareholders, regulators and companies in the 
institution of Independent Directors.
	
The Company has received confirmations from the Directors as 
well as Senior Management Personnel regarding compliance 
of the Code during the year under review.
	
In addition to this, the Company has also adopted the 
separate Code of Conduct for employees of the Company. 
In order to ensure awareness and adherence amongst 
employees, classroom training modules are conducted across 
the Company.

Trading

prohibition of ‘Insider Trading’ known as the Securities and 
Exchange Board of India (Prohibition of Insider Trading) 
Regulations, 2015 (the “Regulations”) which is amended 
from time to time. Further the Companies Act, 2013 has also 
prescribed the provisions on ‘Prohibition on Insider Trading of

Codes viz.

of Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (“UPSI”) to

c)	 Board Procedure
	
The Agenda is circulated well in advance to the Board members. 
The items in the Agenda are backed by comprehensive 
background information to facilitate meaningful discussions 
and enable the Board to take appropriate decisions. As part of 
the process of good governance, the agenda also includes the 
progress on the decisions taken by the Board in its previous 
meeting(s). A Board portal is made available that allows 
Board of Directors to securely access board documents and 
collaborate with other Board members electronically. In case 
any Director(s) seeks additional information, which is not 
part of the information earlier provided, such requests are 
tracked till the actions on such request are addressed to the 
satisfaction of the Director(s) seeking additional information.
	
The Board also, inter-alia, reviews quarterly/half yearly/
annual results, the strategy of business including corporate 
restructuring plans, if any, Annual Operating Plan (“AOP”), 
capital expenditure budgets, update on new business, 
market share of businesses, digital and sustainability viz., 
Environment, Social and Governance initiatives, reports for all 
laws applicable to the Company, review of major legal cases, 
minutes of Meetings of Committee and Board of the Company 
and of Board Meeting of Subsidiary Companies, financials of 
subsidiary companies, review of internal control framework and 
risk management etc. The Directors receive regular updates on 
changes in the relevant laws and regulations which are relevant 
to KOEL at the Board meetings. The required information as 
enumerated in Part A of Schedule II of SEBI Listing Regulations, 
is made available to the Board of Directors for discussions and 
consideration at Board Meetings. Draft Minutes of the Board 
and Committee meetings of the Company are circulated to all 
the Directors for their comments within 15 days of the meeting.

approvals are taken wherever necessary. As a part of corporate 
governance, the Board Charter has been drawn up setting out 
roles/terms of references and processes of functioning of the 
Board including Committees of the Board.
	
The Company has put in place relevant systems and processes 
to ensure compliance with the provisions of applicable laws. In 
accordance with the compliance procedures of the Company, 
relevant Heads of the Departments confirm compliances 
with applicable regulations. The details viz., list of applicable 
laws/rules/regulations, summary of non-compliances, if 
any, including action plan for the same and a certificate duly 
signed by Managing Director is placed before the Board on a 
quarterly basis.

The Company has filed Writ Petition (OS) No. 495 of 2025 - 
Kirloskar Oil Engines Limited & Anr. v. Securities and Exchange 
Board of India ("Writ Petition") before the Hon'ble Bombay 
High Court inter-alia challenging the constitutional validity 
of Regulation 30A read with Clause 5A of Part A of Para A of 
Schedule Ill of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“Regulations”). One of the 
primary contentions taken by the Company in the said Writ 
Petition was that a mere disclosure of an agreement by a 
listed entity, to which such listed entity is not a party, shall not 
automatically bind the listed entity in absence of adoption or 
ratification of such agreement by the listed entity. During the 
course of the hearing in the Writ Petition, SEBI agreed with the 
Company's stand and provided a clarification in the Affidavit in 
Reply filed by SEBI before the Hon'ble Bombay High Court as 
well as the hearing conducted, that the mere disclosure of any 
agreement by a listed entity, shall not, by itself mean that the 
listed entity admits that such agreement is binding on itself or 
as having an impact on its management or control, or imposing 
any restriction or creating any liability upon itself. SEBI further 
clarified that the listed entities may include such a disclaimer 
as a part of their disclosure.
	
Pursuant to and relying upon the aforesaid clarifications issued 
by SEBI to the Regulations, as more particularly contained in 
the Order dated 23rd September, 2025 passed by the Hon'ble 
Bombay High Court in the Writ Petition, the Company disclosed 
the Deed of Family Settlement dated 11th September, 2009, 
entered amongst some of the individual members of the 
Kirloskar family in their individual capacities ("DFS") under the 
Regulations (as read with SEBI’s clarifications) subject to the 
following disclaimers/clarifications:
	
(i)	
The Company states that mere disclosure of the DFS by 
the Company, shall not mean that the Company admits 
to the contents of the DFS or otherwise that such DFS 
is binding on the Company or as having an impact on its 
management or control, or imposing any restriction or 
creating any liability upon itself.
	
(ii)	
The Company expressly states that the Company is 
neither a party to the DFS nor has it ever taken the DFS 
on record nor has it otherwise ratified or approved the 
DFS and neither has it agreed to be bound by the DFS.
	
(iii)	 The Company does not admit that the DFS is binding on 
the Company or that the DFS otherwise in any manner 
has any impact on its management or control, and the 
Company expressly states that the DFS does not impose 
any restriction or create any liability upon the Company 
in any manner whatsoever.

water-use efficiency. These efforts reinforce KOEL's commitment to sustainable water

End Of Life (ELV) regulations do not apply to KOEL products.
	
The Company primarily uses recyclable corrugated boxes and reusable metallic skids for packaging, with minimal particle board usage 
for exports—where metallic skids are retrieved post-delivery. While product recycling is uncommon in this industry, DG sets undergo 
refurbishment to improve efficiency and extend lifespan. Products, mainly composed of high-value metals and alloys like cast iron 
and steel, are typically recycled by customers as metal scrap.
	
As part of our commitment to carbon neutrality, KOEL has launched the Kirloskar Nulife engine programme. We collect engines from

and testing under controlled conditions to meet stringent KOEL quality standards. Nulife engines deliver cost savings, updated 
components, and equivalent performance, durability, and reliability backed by full warranty. Customers benefit from quality-tested, 
remanufactured engines at competitive prices while supporting their carbon reduction targets.

12.	 Describe the measures taken by the entity to ensure a safe and healthy work place.
	
The Company is committed to providing and maintaining a safe and healthy workplace through a robust occupational health and 
safety management framework. During the year, external audits covering plant safety, fire safety, electrical systems, and ventilation 
were conducted across facilities by competent agencies. In addition, various safety and health awareness and training programmes 
were organised to strengthen the safety culture across the organisation.
	
Key initiatives undertaken by the Company include:
	y Training and Capacity Building: Regular training programmes are conducted to enhance employee awareness of workplace 
hazards, safe work practices, and emergency response procedures.
	y Safety Inspections and Audits: Periodic safety inspections and internal as well as external audits are undertaken to identify 
potential risks and implement corrective and preventive actions.
	y Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): Appropriate PPE, such as helmets, gloves, safety glasses, respirators, and other 
protective gear, is provided based on the nature of work and associated risks.
	y Hierarchy of Controls: Workplace hazards are managed through a structured approach comprising elimination, substitution, 
engineering controls, administrative controls, and the use of PPE.
	y Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment: The Company conducts Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA), Job 
Safety Analysis (JSA), and on-the-job safety training to proactively identify and mitigate operational risks.
	y Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) System: A formal LOTO procedure is implemented to ensure the safe isolation and control of 
hazardous energy sources during maintenance and repair activities.
	y Work Permit System: Critical and high-risk activities are governed through a structured Work Permit System to ensure 
compliance with established safety protocols.
	y Hazard and Operability Studies (HAZOP): HAZOP studies are carried out for critical operations and processes to identify 
potential hazards and strengthen risk mitigation measures.
	
Through these initiatives, the Company continues to foster a culture of safety and operational excellence while striving to prevent 
workplace injuries and occupational health incidents.

received from stakeholders on these topics were incorporated into the policies and activities of

Stakeholder engagement is a fundamental element of KOEL's approach to identifying, assessing, and managing environmental, 
social, and governance (ESG) risks and opportunities. Building on the materiality assessment conducted in FY 2023, the Company 
carried out a comprehensive materiality reassessment in FY 2026 to validate the relevance of previously identified material topics 
and ensure alignment with evolving stakeholder expectations, regulatory requirements, and the changing business landscape. The 
reassessment followed a structured and systematic methodology, with stakeholder perspectives serving as a key input throughout 
the process.
	
As part of the reassessment, KOEL engaged a broad spectrum of internal and external stakeholders, including the Board of 
Directors, senior leadership, employees, customers, suppliers, investors, regulators, industry associations, local communities, 
NGOs, and knowledge partners. Stakeholder feedback was primarily gathered through structured surveys designed to evaluate 
the significance of identified ESG topics. The responses were assessed using a robust scoring methodology, and the outcomes 
were used to update the Company's materiality matrix, providing a strong foundation for its sustainability priorities.
	
The insights generated through this engagement process have been integrated into KOEL's governance and sustainability 
framework. Stakeholder feedback has strengthened the incorporation of ESG considerations into enterprise risk management, 
strategic planning, and business decision-making, enabling the Company to proactively address emerging risks and opportunities. 
The findings of the FY 2026 reassessment are also guiding the development of KOEL's Sustainability Strategy 2030 by defining 
priority focus areas, establishing measurable Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), and setting long-term sustainability objectives.

The helpdesk operates on a 24/7 basis, ensuring uninterrupted assistance. In emergency situations, helpdesk personnel facilitate

To ensure service quality and accountability, all customer service requests are systematically recorded and tracked through the 
Dealer Business Management System (Pulse) until successful resolution. For post-warranty concerns, customers may reach out to 
authorised service dealers, who log and manage such requests within the Pulse system.
	
The Company follows a structured approach to grievance redressal, with customer complaints handled by designated personnel, 
including Area Service Managers, Rapid Response Teams (RRT), Zonal Service Managers, and Key Account Managers. These 
representatives engage directly with customers to understand concerns and initiate corrective actions through the service dealer 
network. Where required, in-person interactions are undertaken to ensure effective resolution. In addition, targeted service campaigns 
are conducted to proactively identify and address segment-specific issues, enabling continuous improvement in systems and products.
	
The Company leverages digital and technological capabilities to strengthen customer engagement and after-sales service. Key 
Performance Indicators (KPIs), including response time (within 4 hours), turnaround time for repairs (24–48 hours), First Time Right 
(FTR), and First Visit Resolution (FVR), are closely monitored through the Pulse system to ensure adherence to service standards and 
drive continuous improvement.
	
Service requests are allocated to relevant service dealers based on pin code mapping within Pulse. Progress is monitored daily across 
all levels, from service dealers to the Customer Support leadership, with defined escalation timelines for ageing requests to ensure 
timely closure.

Executive Summary
In today’s dynamic industrial environment shaped by climate change, 
technological evolution, and geopolitical shifts, robust supply chain 
resilience and sustainability have become strategic priorities. For 
engineered solutions providers like Kirloskar Oil Engines Limited 
(“KOEL”/“Company”), these drivers pose both challenges and 
opportunities: innovation cycles are accelerating, ESG regulations 
are tightening, and disruptions, from supply shocks to regulatory 
changes, are emerging more frequently. As a result, KOEL is moving 
beyond conventional cost-driven approaches to embrace value-led, 
ecosystem-based sourcing strategies that enhance transparency, 
trust, and long-term competitiveness.
Resilience and sustainability underpin KOEL’s supply chain ethos. 
Operating across critical sectors such as manufacturing, oil & 
gas, power, and refrigeration, KOEL recognises its responsibility 
to reduce emissions, manage resources responsibly, and ensure 
ethical supplier practices. Our ESG Policy that is aligned with global 
frameworks extends to value chain ensuring our partners adopt 
best-in-class environmental, social, and governance standards.
This Value Chain Report (“Report”) has been structured to disclose 
the performance of our value chain against the BRSR Core framework, 
a streamlined version of the broader sustainability reporting standard 
by Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI). Pursuant to SEBI 
Circular No. SEBI/HO/CFD/CFD-PoD-1/P/CIR/2025/42 dated 28th 
March, 2025, the requirement for disclosing and assuring value chain 
data that has been deferred by one year, with the reporting boundary 
now covering partners contributing 2% to the purchases or sales 
value, cumulatively covering up to 75% of total value.
KOEL is utilising this extended timeline to further reinforce ESG due 
diligence across its value chain and enhance the availability, quality, 
and consistency of supplier level ESG data. Through structured 
collaboration with its suppliers, KOEL aims to identify and mitigate 
potential ESG risks, promote continuous improvement, and ensure 
preparedness for future regulatory requirements, while collectively 
driving long term value creation and sustainable development.
ESG Commitment and Governance
KOEL demonstrates a strong commitment to Environmental, Social, 
and Governance (ESG) excellence through a structured ESG framework 
that integrates sustainability into its business strategy, operations, 
and value chain. The Company emphasises minimising environmental 
impact by advancing energy efficiency, expanding renewable energy 
use, conserving water, promoting circularity, and reducing emissions, 
including achieving carbon-neutral milestones at key facilities. Its 
governance practices are anchored in transparency, ethical conduct, 
robust risk management, and compliance with national guidelines 
and global reporting standards such as GRI, supported by external 
assurance to ensure credibility. KOEL’s ESG approach also prioritises 
employee well-being, workplace safety, human rights, and inclusive 
employment practices while fostering strong stakeholder 
engagement. Through responsible sourcing, increased collaboration 
with local and MSME suppliers, and initiatives to build a resilient, low-
carbon supply chain, the Company strengthens accountability and 
operational continuity. With long-term sustainability goals aligned to 
its 2030 strategy, KOEL continues to advance climate stewardship, 
resource efficiency, and community development, reflecting a holistic 
and future ready ESG governance model.
Approach to Supplier Engagement and Data 
Collection
KOEL’s approach follows a structured methodology to gather 
data against the BRSR Core framework.
1.	
Supplier Prioritisation: Identification of suppliers meeting 
SEBI-defined value thresholds (≥2% procurement value), 
covering up to 75% of total procurement spend.
2.	
Structured data collection: Deployment of standardised 
questionnaires based on BRSR Core environmental, social, 
and governance indicators.
3.	
Capacity Building: Conducted BRSR Core sensitisation 
workshops covering a detailed walkthrough of the nine Core 
indicators and their computation.
Reporting Scope
This Report has been prepared in accordance with the SEBI BRSR 
Core framework and covers upstream value chain partners that 
meet the revised materiality thresholds prescribed under the SEBI 
Circular dated 28th March, 2025. The reporting boundary has been 
carefully defined to ensure accuracy, comparability, and consistency 
across all indicators evaluated.
For FY 2024–25, KOEL’s total procurement spend stood at C 1,12,752 
Lakhs. In accordance with the regulatory requirement to include value 
chain partners contributing ≥2% of annual procurement spend; the 
assessment boundary includes suppliers meeting this threshold. This 
assessment identified 6 suppliers who accounted for 2% or more of the 
total procurement spend. We have received partial information from 
few suppliers who independently meet the SEBI-defined threshold; 
however, this data has not been included in the current Report to 
maintain consistency across indicators and avoid reporting gaps that 
could arise due to incomplete submissions. The scope of the Report 
presents complete and verifiable BRSR Core information of suppliers 
who account for 56% of KOEL’s procurement spend; given that these 
partners are publicly listed entities, the required supplier information 
was sourced from publicly available disclosures.
KOEL is committed to building the readiness of its suppliers and 
is actively engaging with them to support their ability to collect, 
maintain, and report BRSR-aligned data in future reporting cycles.

Introduction and objective of engagement
Kirloskar Oil Engines Limited (the 'Company') has developed its 
Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) 2025-
26 (the ‘Report’) based on the BRSR reporting guidelines, including 
the BRSR Core indicators prescribed by SEBI for listed entities. 
The reporting criteria have been derived from the Principles of 
National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct (NGRBC), 
and Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol - A Corporate Accounting and 
Reporting Standard.
BDO India Services Private Limited (“BDO India”) was engaged by 
the Company to provide independent assurance on BRSR Core 
indicators of the Report that includes the Company’s performance 
for the period 1st April 2025 through 31st March 2026.
The Company’s responsibilities
The Report content and its presentation are the sole responsibilities 
of the management of the Company. The Company management is 
also responsible for the design, implementation, and maintenance 
of internal controls relevant to the preparation of the Report, so that 
it is free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.
BDO India’s responsibilities
BDO India’s responsibility, as agreed with the management of the 
Company, is to provide assurance on the Report content as described 
in the ‘Scope, boundary & assurance criteria’ section below. We do 
not accept or assume any responsibility for any other purpose or 
to any other person or organisation. Any reliance a third party may 
place on the Report is entirely at its own risk.
Assurance standard
We conducted our assurance engagement in accordance with 
International Standard on Assurance Engagements (ISAE) 3000 
(Revised), “Assurance Engagements Other than Audits or Reviews 
of Historical Financial Information” and ISAE 3410, “Assurance 
Engagements on Greenhouse Gas Statement” issued by the 
International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB).
Scope, boundary & assurance criteria
The reporting scope and boundary cover the Company’s 
standalone operations.
We applied the ‘Reasonable’ Assurance criteria for non-financial 
BRSR Core Indicators1, pertaining to the Company’s disclosure for 
the period 1st April 2025 through 31st March 2026.
Verification of non-financial sustainability performance data, based 
on our professional judgement was conducted at the following sites:
Onsite Verification:
	y Kirloskar Oil Engines Limited, Nashik, Maharashtra
	y Kirloskar Oil Engines Limited, Kagal, Kolhapur, Maharashtra
	y Kirloskar Oil Engines Limited, Khadki, Pune, Maharashtra
Online Verification:
	y Kirloskar Oil Engines Limited, Bhare, Pune, Maharashtra
	y Kirloskar Oil Engines Limited, Rajkot, Gujarat
Assurance methodology
Our assurance process entails conducting procedures to gather 
evidence regarding the reliability of the disclosures covered in the 
assurance scope. We conducted a review and verification of data 
collection, collation, and calculation methodologies, and a general 
review of the logic of inclusion/ omission of relevant information/ 
data in the Report. Our review process included:
	y Evaluation and assessment of the appropriateness of the 
quantification methods used to arrive at the non-financial 
sustainability information of the BRSR Core indicators in 
the Report;
	y Review of consistency of data/information within the Report 
as well as between the Report and the source;
	y Engagement through discussions with personnel at the 
corporate level who are accountable for the data and 
information presented in the Report;
	y Execution of an audit trail of claims and data streams, to 
determine the level of accuracy in collection, transcription, 
and aggregation;
	y Review of data collection and management procedures, and 
related internal controls;
